source.title: What if I ask in alia lingua? Measuring Functional Similarity Across Languages
source.authors: Debangan Mishra; Arihant Rastogi; Agyeya Negi; Shashwat Goel; P. Kumaraguru

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses representational similarity and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but its main scale results measure functional output agreement across languages, not the representational convergence or model comparisons specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study measures functional consistency across languages and reports its relationship to model size, accuracy, domain, language resources, and other metrics. Those are related findings, but functional output agreement is not the representational convergence named in V1–V7. It also reports a limited association between functional similarity and representational cosine similarity, without testing representational convergence with scale or between independently trained models.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the Platonic Representation Hypothesis as motivation, but it measures something else. It looks at functional output agreement (κp, Cohen's κ, Scott's π) on GlobalMMLU multiple-choice answers, and mostly within a single model across languages. It does not measure representational alignment between independently trained models as a function of scale. Its only representational analysis (Appendix E) is within one model across languages, for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B only, with no numbers. None of V1–V7 is tested, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. Larger and more capable models are more consistent across languages. Intra-model similarity exceeds inter-model similarity. Consistency is higher in STEM and for high-resource languages. Functional and representational similarity correlate somewhat. Causality is not established.
record.recipe_differences: Measures multilingual functional agreement in model outputs with κp and related agreement metrics; it does not apply the original representational similarity method. The representational comparison uses cosine similarity on sentence representations.
record.method_sensitivity: Functional κp differs by question domain, with STEM tending to be higher; language resource availability correlates with inter-model similarity. The authors report that findings persist under Cohen’s κ and Scott’s π and in an English-pivot ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-model functional output consistency across languages correlates with model size (κp r=0.786, p=0.021) and accuracy (r=0.788). The same holds, more strongly, under Cohen's κ and Scott's π.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger, more accurate LLMs give more functionally consistent answers across languages on parallel MCQ benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-model cross-language κp exceeds inter-model same-language κp for all 8 models (Mann–Whitney p<0.001 under κp). This holds in an English-pivot ablation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models agree more with themselves across languages than with other models in the same language.

fits_no_version.finding: Inter-model functional agreement correlates with language resource availability (r=0.923 with log Wikipedia article count). Within-model agreement is higher for STEM than for culturally sensitive subjects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Functional agreement depends on language resources and question domain.

fits_no_version.finding: Language pairs with higher κp show higher baseline-adjusted last-token cosine similarity (Qwen3-4B and 8B, FLORES-101). No number is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-language functional and representational similarity within a model are associated.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 5th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2025)
record.problems: The principal results are limited to multiple-choice functional output agreement on GlobalMMLU. The authors state that they cannot establish causality and do not have access to the models’ exact training data. The representational comparison is limited to Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, limited layers, and FLORES-101; no numerical association or uncertainty is stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the study’s related functional-similarity findings were omitted.

untested.parts: Representational alignment across independently trained models as size grows. The scale trend reported is only for functional within-model cross-language consistency.
Metric dependence of representational convergence. The metric comparison concerns functional agreement only.
Plateau of representational alignment, and causes from shared data or objectives. The authors only speculate about training data.

record.verdict_notes: Cited as motivation, PRH (Huh et al. 2024) is not an object of the study's test. Inter-model functional agreement is never related to model scale, so the study gives no output-space analogue of V1 between models either. The 'results consistent across metrics' claim has one non-significant exception: Qwen3-1.7B under Cohen's κ (p=0.061).

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether representations of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, and data become more aligned as model size and capability grow.
Does not compare vision and language models or paired images and captions.
Does not compare networks trained from different initializations or measure shared features or subspaces.
Does not test mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired interchangeability between models.
Does not identify recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
Compares metrics and input domains for functional output similarity, not whether measured representational convergence depends on metric settings or inputs, or weakens out of distribution.
Does not test whether representational alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives explain it.
